topic: How AI Learns to Reason: Reward Models & Thinking
description: Check your understanding of reasoning-oriented generation, DeepSeek-style models, Chain of Thought, RLVF vs RLHF, evaluators, ToT/GoT, and the limits of more thinking.

questions.question: What is reasoning-oriented generation?
options: Only training on more Common Crawl pages
Working through a problem step-by-step before answering, not just guessing the next word
Always answering in one token
questions.explanation: The notes contrast fast pattern-based replies with breaking a question into pieces, weighing options, and checking logic — like solving a riddle instead of shouting a guess.

questions.question: A company grows revenue 20% then loses 20%. What is the net change?
options: 0% — they cancel out
4% decrease (final is 96% of original)
20% increase
questions.explanation: 120% then 80% of 120 is 96%. Direct generation might say 0%; a reasoning path computes the composition.

questions.question: When is long thinking most useful?
options: Every greeting like 'hi'
Reasoning-oriented tasks (plan, edge cases, debug, tests) — not every direct-generation question
Only during pre-training, never at inference
questions.explanation: For simple direct generation, extra thinking may add no value. For complex work, inference-time deliberation matters.

questions.question: What do reasoning models try to do at inference time?
options: Skip the answer and only crawl the web
Bring deliberate computation into answering: understand, consider cases, then reply
Delete the reward model
questions.explanation: Easy words in the notes: they pause to think and work through complex problems step-by-step before giving an answer.

questions.question: Is Reinforcement Learning a brand-new idea from DeepSeek R1?
options: Yes, it was invented in 2025 for chatbots only
No — RL is older; AlphaGo used it and beat a Go expert 4–1 in 2016
RL can only be used in military robots
questions.explanation: The episode stresses RL is not new. AlphaGo is the landmark example before LLM reasoning models.

questions.question: Google Brain and DeepMind — which is true?
options: They were always one team called OpenAI
Separate Google AI labs that merged in 2023 into Google DeepMind
DeepMind only makes phone cameras
questions.explanation: Brain (2011, products/data) and DeepMind (2014, AGI/games/science) officially merged in 2023.

questions.question: What is Chain of Thought?
options: A type of GPU
Writing intermediate reasoning steps before the final answer
Only crawling FineWeb
questions.explanation: CoT is the named technique for step-by-step traces (paper 2201.11903). Same idea as the puzzles in the episode.

questions.question: Does more thinking guarantee a correct answer?
options: Yes, always
No — it can raise probability but not certainty; overthinking can even hurt
Only if the model is DeepSeek
questions.explanation: Notes: more thinking is not infinitely useful. Overthinking can bring diminishing returns or drop a correct first solution.

questions.question: What is RLVF / RLVR?
options: The same as Common Crawl
Reinforcement from verifiable feedback/reward — a program checks a clear right/wrong outcome
A type of tokenizer
questions.explanation: Math, chess, and unit tests can be auto-scored. No human needed for those rewards, unlike subjective RLHF.

questions.question: How should you map RLHF vs RLVF?
options: Subjective preference → humans → RLHF; verifiable answer → rules/computer → RLVF/RLVR
They are identical acronyms
RLVF only works on travel itineraries
questions.explanation: 5+5 and chess are verifiable; a travel plan is not. That split is the point of the episode.

questions.question: Which evaluator uses an exact check like unit tests or a compiler?
options: Human evaluator
Deterministic evaluator
Only LLM-as-a-Judge
questions.explanation: Three judges: deterministic (exact/tests/schema), human, and model (LLM-as-a-Judge). Deterministic is best when possible.

questions.question: What is a known issue with LLM-as-a-Judge?
options: It can never run on a GPU
Biases such as position bias — where an answer sits can change the score
It always matches human experts perfectly
questions.explanation: The notes flag biases and reliability problems even though LLM judges are trending.

questions.question: Tree of Thoughts (ToT) is best described as:
options: Trying multiple reasoning paths, checking work, and backtracking if a path fails
Training only on HTML
A replacement for tokenization
questions.explanation: ToT is a different style of CoT that explores a tree of ideas, like a human on a hard puzzle.

questions.question: Graph of Thoughts (GoT) differs from a straight CoT line because it:
options: Forbids any intermediate steps
Links ideas as nodes so thoughts can mix, loop, and combine
Only works for image models
questions.explanation: GoT is a network of interconnected thoughts, closer to mixing ideas than a single chain.

questions.question: Visible reasoning traces (the 'thinking' text) are:
options: Always a faithful log of the model's true internal computation
Not necessarily faithful
Required by law to be 100% accurate
questions.explanation: The notes say visible reasoning is not necessarily faithful.

questions.question: What three factors does the episode say make capable systems possible?
options: CSS, HTML, and JavaScript
Knowledge + Reasoning + Tools
Only more pre-training tokens
questions.explanation: Closing line of the episode: knowledge, reasoning, and tools together. Tools are teased for later.
